title: Uncle Ray's Swordfish Steak
intro: This spontaneous, intuition-driven swordfish recipe was inspired by a quick trip to Trader Joe's. It features a unique soju deglaze and an experimental miso-apple garnish, proving that culinary improvisation can yield surprisingly elegant results.

steps.title: Preheat the pan
steps.instruction: Heat up a pan significantly until it is very hot. To test the heat, drop a little water onto the surface; it is sufficiently heated when the water creates the Leidenfrost effect (dancing rapidly on the surface).

steps.title: Mix the miso glaze
steps.instruction: In a bowl, mix the miso paste, soy sauce, and mirin until the paste becomes liquid and easy to pour. Add a splash of water to help it combine, then season with a pinch of salt and some black pepper. Stir in the honey, making sure to scrape the edges of the bowl as the honey tends to stick to the bottom. Add more miso if the mixture is too salty or tart.

steps.title: Prepare the garlic and green onion garnish
steps.instruction: Crush a garlic clove by pressing the flat side of a knife over it, then give it a rough chop. Next, trim off the overly bendy part of a green onion stalk so only the firm, light green section remains. Cut this section in half to get long strips, then slice them lengthwise very thinly. Place these thin strips into a bowl of ice-cold water to blanch them, which will cause them to curl up elegantly for the garnish. Check your preheated pan with a few drops of water again to ensure it's hot enough.

steps.title: Start searing the swordfish
steps.instruction: Add vegetable oil to the hot pan. Place the swordfish steak in the pan and press it down firmly to ensure it develops a good sear. Turn the heat down slightly so it doesn't char too aggressively. After a couple of minutes, flip the steak over, turn the heat down further, and aggressively deglaze the pan with a little bit of soju.

steps.title: Sear all sides and cool the pan
steps.instruction: Turn the heat back up a little bit and press the fish down again. You will know a good sear has formed when the fish can move easily in the pan. Carefully flip the steak to sear all the remaining edges so none of the outside is left unseared. Once it has developed a bit of char, remove the fish from the heat and turn the stove down completely to let the hot pan cool, which prevents the butter from burning in the next step.

steps.title: Cook the apples in soju and miso glaze
steps.instruction: Add the pre-sliced apples to the pan, separating the pieces nicely so they cook evenly. Pour soju over the apples and let it cook down until the smell of alcohol disappears. Pour in the prepared miso glaze and let it reduce while the apples soften in the pan. Taste an apple slice and remove any pieces that have become too mushy. Once cooked, remove all the apple slices from the pan and turn the heat up to thicken the remaining glaze.

steps.instruction: Using a small spoon, place the reduced miso sauce onto the center of a plate and spread it into a neat circle. Remove the large pieces of garlic and thyme from the rested swordfish steak, and set the fish down on top of the sauce. Carefully place the rolled apple roses next to the fish. Take the curled green onion strips out of the ice water, pat them dry with a paper towel, and arrange them elegantly on top of the swordfish. Finally, wipe the edges of the plate clean with a paper towel.

stories.title: Trader Joe's Inspiration
stories.text: I kind of just went to Trader Joe's today to see what they had. Uh and they had a swordfish steak, which was pretty interesting. I like to go to Trader Joe's and just find anything that's interesting to me. And today what stood out were some green apples and uh a swordfish steak. So I thought I'd plan everything around that.

stories.title: Cooking Without a Recipe
stories.text: I started cooking like two months ago when I moved into this place uh just because like I thought it'd be fun. Um and like I actually didn't expect to like it as much as I do. But every day or like every every couple weeks I just kind of go to Trader Joe's and just get whatever and then I just like make some bullshit. Um so that's kind of my philosophy. I think like I like to do things without a recipe as well. Like I did not really look up swordfish recipes for this. I have no idea what swordfish should be cooked like.

stories.title: The Chicago River Swordfish Fantasy
stories.text: And for the sake of the video I'll just say that this is like a really old family recipe that my family has been cultivating for centuries. You know, yeah, we catch our swordfish live in Chicago. You think swordfish run in like the Chicago River? Like the river that comes through the city? Yeah, definitely not, but it's kind of a personal fantasy of mine right now. Like as of right now I've developed this fantasy that there are swordfish in the river.

stories.title: Cooking Isn't Intimidating
stories.text: I think people kind of find cooking really intimidating, but honestly, anything that you put in a pan is probably going to be valid. Um, I think it's actually harder to like really, really mess something up rather than just like kind of do whatever. Um, for instance, like the ingredients that you use will all still be like yummy, you know.

stories.text: I have no idea how cooked the inside is and honestly, that's fine. Um, I'm okay with eating raw meat. I think it should make my immune system stronger. I don't think salmonella is real. It's got to be like propaganda at this point. Yeah, yeah, I agree. They just don't want you eating like cookie batter and stuff. Yeah, yeah, yeah. It's like yeah. They don't want you to be happy.

stories.text: Caleb has some disagreements. He thinks I'm pretty autistic. Um, I can see the reasoning behind it... Yeah, like I just like fully messed that up, but you know, whatever. Yeah, I got fully messed that up, but like whatever. ... Okay, I'm in flow state.

stories.title: Culinary LARP
stories.text: The cook looks at the blanched onions and reflects on culinary terminology, saying that blanching is just putting things in cold water so they curl up, and that a lot of cooking involves giving weird names to simple processes, like calling fruit in a pan a "compote." He concludes that a lot of it is just "larp."

stories.title: Optimal Cooking Music
stories.text: I'm a big fan of R&B when I'm cooking. Like I think it's like optimal cooking music.

special.text: The cook deglazes the pan with soju instead of wine or broth.
special.why: Soju is a Korean distilled beverage, not typically used for deglazing a pan-seared fish steak in Western cooking, though it might be used in some Asian cuisines to remove fishy odors.

special.text: The cook decides to blanch the finely chopped green onions 'for fun' without knowing what it will do to them.
special.why: Green onions used as garnish are typically served raw for their crisp texture and sharp flavor; blanching them after chopping is highly unusual and defeats the purpose of a fresh garnish.

follow_up_questions.question: You added sliced apples to the pan, but we never saw them being cut. About how many apples did you slice, and how thinly should they be cut to properly form the roses?
The microgreens were thrown out because they were soggy, but if they had been fresh, at what stage of plating would you have added them?
When checking the pan's heat with water, you mentioned it was sizzling and not dancing. Did you wait for the pan to get hotter before adding the oil and swordfish in later steps?
